name: Common Noun Phrase

1.definition: NP whose nominal head is a common noun; compatible with definite or indefinite, and unique or non-unique, reference

examples.note: Specific reference to a set of books

constraints.description: The nominal head must be a common noun

relatedConstructions.notes: Dogs can be both bare and headed by a common noun. The dogs has the same head category with an overt determiner.
The dogs is both determined and headed by a common noun. Dogs has the same head category without an overt determiner.

projection.target: A common noun such as river heads either the river or a river. A particular identifiable referent need not therefore be named through a proper noun.
projection.evidence: CGEL contrasts the lexical noun classes and distinguishes referential status from noun class.

curious.title: Phrases built on everyday nouns
curious.summary: A common noun phrase is built around an ordinary noun like river or book, not a name.
curious.body: Ordinary nouns such as dog, river and book head phrases like the books or a river. A phrase like this can point to something definite or something indefinite, and to one particular thing or to something less specific. So a particular, identifiable thing doesn't have to be named with a name. The river can point to one particular river, and the books to a set of books.
curious.try: Think of something you can point to in the room. Can you refer to it without using a name?

teacher.summary: Separates the kind of noun heading a phrase from whether the phrase is definite or identifies one referent.
teacher.explain: A common noun phrase has a common noun as its nominal head. It's compatible with definite or indefinite reference and with unique or non-unique reference. The noun class and the referential status are different matters: a noun such as river heads either the river or a river, so a particular identifiable referent need not be named with a proper noun. Dogs and the dogs share the same head category; the first has no overt determiner and the second has one.
watch_for: A learner might think a definite NP has to contain a proper noun.
A learner might think a common noun phrase must contain a determiner.
